title: Migrating Google ADK to Telemetry Schema v2 Silently Broke Every Analytics Query
author: Hiroshi Toyama
summary: Upgrading Google ADK from 2.7 to 2.13, I also flipped telemetry from ADK's own schema v1 to schema v2, which follows the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions. The upgrade itself was uneventful. What was not: every BigQuery query reading our Cloud Trace spans started returning zero rows. No errors, no warnings. WHERE name = 'call_llm' simply stopped matching anything, because that span no longer exists. Here are the six traps I hit, in the order they cost me time. The setup: spans read from BigQuery Some context on the pipeline, because it explains why the breakage was silent. Agent spans go to Cloud Trace, and we query them from BigQuery with SQL. We want to aggregate "which agent, with what instruction, what the user said, what the model answered" after the fact, so eyeballing the trace UI is not enough. Agent (Cloud Run) │ OTel spans ▼ SpanProcessor wrapper ── shrinks attributes over 64 KiB │ export ▼ Cloud Trace _Trace bucket (30-day retention) │ │ google_observability_link ▼ BigQuery dataset: cloud_trace_spans └── _AllSpans (a VIEW — no copy of the data) │ bq query --location=us ▼ analytics queries A common misreading: this is not a Logging sink. Nothing is routed through the log router into BigQuery. It is a linked dataset attached to Cloud Trace's _Trace bucket: resource "google_observability_link" "cloud_trace_spans" { location = "us" bucket = "_Trace" dataset = "Spans" link_id = "cloud_trace_spans" } # The link needs BigQuery permission on the observability service agent resource "google_project_iam_member" "observability_bigquery_admin" { project = var . project_id role = "roles/bigquery.admin" member = "serviceAccount:service-${data.google_project.project.number}@gcp-sa-observability.iam.gserviceaccount.com" } Three properties of this setup matter later: _AllSpans is a VIEW, not a table. No data is copied, so retention follows Cloud Trace (30 days by default). There is no "dig into last year's data". The dataset lives in us . Without --location=us , bq query tells you the dataset does not exist. All span attributes arrive in a single JSON column called attributes . So every analytics query looks like this: SELECT JSON_VALUE ( attributes , '$."gen_ai.input.messages"' ) AS input FROM `<project>.cloud_trace_spans._AllSpans` WHERE start_time >= TIMESTAMP_SUB ( CURRENT_TIMESTAMP (), INTERVAL 7 DAY ) That last property is the direct cause of the incident. JSON paths have no schema and no type checking. Point JSON_VALUE at a key that does not exist and it returns NULL without complaint. Misspell a real column name and BigQuery stops you instantly; misspell a JSON path and it says nothing at all. So when schema v2 renamed every attribute, the queries kept succeeding and started returning zero rows. That is how an entire analytics pipeline breaks without anyone noticing. What actually changes Schema v2 is gated behind ADK_TELEMETRY_SCHEMA_VERSION_OPT_IN=2 . The mapping: v1 v2 LLM call span call_llm generate_content <model> Agent span invocation / agent_run [name] invoke_agent <name> / invoke_workflow <name> Tool span execute_tool <name> execute_tool <name> (unchanged) LLM request body gcp.vertex.agent.llm_request gen_ai.input.messages LLM response body gcp.vertex.agent.llm_response gen_ai.output.messages System instruction inside llm_request gen_ai.system_instructions Tool definitions inside llm_request gen_ai.tool.definitions Tool arguments gcp.vertex.agent.tool_call_args gen_ai.tool.call.arguments Tool result gcp.vertex.agent.tool_response gen_ai.tool.call.result Agent name embedded in span name gen_ai.agent.name v1 stuffs whole JSON blobs into single attributes; v2 splits them by meaning. The direction is right, but every reference you have breaks at once. Note the dots in gen_ai.tool.definitions . I wrote gen_ai.tool_definitions in a design doc and nobody caught it until someone ran it. Pull the constant instead of trusting your memory: from opentelemetry.semconv._incubating.attributes import gen_ai_attributes as g print ( g . GEN_AI_TOOL_DEFINITIONS ) # gen_ai.tool.definitions Trap 1: without SPAN_ONLY, no content is recorded at all This one cost the most. After switching to v2, spans appeared but every content attribute was empty. In v2, content capture is governed by the OTel-side variable OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT : Value Behavior NO_CONTENT (default) Records nothing SPAN_ONLY Records into span attributes EVENT_ONLY Records into log records (OTel events) SPAN_AND_EVENT Both ADK's own ADK_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT_IN_SPANS=true is a v1-only knob . If you migrated from v1, that one is probably already set to true , which makes the failure look especially confusing: the setting is right there, and nothing is captured. The tempting choice is SPAN_AND_EVENT — why not have both? Because the event path needs a LoggerProvider , and ADK only creates one when log record processors exist: # google/adk/telemetry/setup.py if log_record_processors : # LoggerProvider is created only here ... If you call get_gcp_exporters(enable_cloud_tracing=True) and nothing else, you have zero log record processors, so there is no LoggerProvider and nowhere for those events to go. For a trace-only setup, SPAN_ONLY is the only sensible value: env { name = "OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT" value = "SPAN_ONLY" } env { name = "ADK_TELEMETRY_SCHEMA_VERSION_OPT_IN" value = "2" } Trap 2: v1 and v2 bodies live in different ROWS, not different columns During a migration you have both schemas in the same table, so you reach for a fallback: -- This does nothing useful COALESCE ( JSON_VALUE ( attributes , '$."gcp.vertex.agent.llm_request"' ), JSON_VALUE ( attributes , '$."gen_ai.input.messages"' ) ) AS llm_input COALESCE picks the first non-NULL within one row . But the v1 body sits on a call_llm row and the v2 body sits on a generate_content ... row. The two attributes never coexist in a single row, so this expression only ever returns whichever one that row already had. It is a fallback that cannot fall back. Branch on the span name and treat them as separate rows: WHERE name = 'call_llm' OR STARTS_WITH ( name , 'generate_content ' ) And extract differently per shape: CASE WHEN name = 'call_llm' THEN -- v1: llm_request.contents[last].parts[].text ( SELECT STRING_AGG ( JSON_VALUE ( pt , '$.text' ), ' / ' ) FROM UNNEST ( JSON_QUERY_ARRAY ( last_content , '$.parts' )) AS pt ) ELSE -- v2: input_messages[last].parts[].content ( SELECT STRING_AGG ( JSON_VALUE ( pt , '$.content' ), ' / ' ) FROM UNNEST ( JSON_QUERY_ARRAY ( last_message , '$.parts' )) AS pt ) END AS user_text The inner keys differ too: a v1 part uses text , a v2 part uses content . The assistant role is model in v1 and assistant in v2, per semconv. Meanwhile, tool arguments and results do share a row, because execute_tool <name> keeps the same span name across both schemas. There, COALESCE is exactly right: COALESCE ( JSON_VALUE ( attributes , '$."gcp.vertex.agent.tool_call_args"' ), JSON_VALUE ( attributes , '$."gen_ai.tool.call.arguments"' ) ) AS tool_args So the same migration needs two different fallback strategies depending on which span you are reading. You will not deduce this from the docs; you have to capture real spans and look. Trap 3: resolving the agent name needs parent traversal, not trace_id v1 embedded the agent in the span name ( agent_run [SomeLeafAgent] ). v2 exposes gen_ai.agent.name as its own attribute — but it is not on v1's call_llm . To cover both during migration, walk up the parent chain: SELECT b . * , COALESCE ( JSON_VALUE ( b . attributes , '$."gen_ai.agent.name"' ), JSON_VALUE ( p . attributes , '$."gen_ai.agent.name"' ), JSON_VALUE ( g . attributes , '$."gen_ai.agent.name"' ) ) AS agent_name FROM base b LEFT JOIN base p ON b . parent_span_id = p . span_id -- parent LEFT JOIN base g ON p . parent_span_id = g . span_id -- grandparent Do not join on trace_id . A single trace contains the router agent and any AgentTool children, so a trace-wide join happily attributes one agent's spans to another. In practice, every v2 generate_content span in my capture carried gen_ai.agent.name directly. The parent traversal is insurance for the v1 rows during the overlap window. Trap 4: the 64 KiB attribute limit rejects the whole batch GCP's Telemetry API refuses any attribute over 64 KiB — and it does not drop just that attribute. The entire batch comes back HTTP 400. One oversized system instruction erases every span that shipped with it. v1 was easy to trip because it packed everything into one attribute. v2 does not really help: gen_ai.system_instructions and gen_ai.tool.definitions get large on their own. Mine reached 63,427 bytes. The obvious lever, OTel SDK's OTEL_ATTRIBUTE_VALUE_LENGTH_LIMIT , is the wrong tool. It truncates by character count with no UTF-8 byte guarantee, and it cuts JSON mid-structure, so what survives no longer parses. Unparseable bodies are worthless for analytics. I wrapped ADK's span processors instead, shrinking attributes with knowledge of the JSON structure just before export: wrapped_hooks = OTelHooks ( span_processors = [ SpanAttributeLimitSpanProcessor ( p ) for p in hooks . span_processors ], metric_readers = list ( hooks . metric_readers ), log_record_processors = list ( hooks . log_record_processors ), ) maybe_set_otel_providers ([ wrapped_hooks ], resource ) Wrapping rather than replacing the exporter keeps ADK's native Cloud Trace batching. The shrink order goes by analytic value: incidental fields like grounding_metadata and logprobs_result first, then tool definitions, then the system instruction, then oldest conversation turns. A __adk_span_truncated__ marker always goes in so downstream readers know. In production it looks like this: WARNING Truncated span attribute: span=generate_content gemini-3.8-flash attribute=gen_ai.system_instructions original_bytes=63427 63 KB shrank to 27,826 characters with the tail (the most recent context) preserved, and zero 400s since. One known weakness: this approach handles one huge string well and many medium strings badly. When no single removal gets you under budget, the depth-first shrink gives up and collapses everything to the marker. I reproduced 30 parts x 2.1 KB = 63,520 bytes — only 3.5 KB over budget — degrading to 47 bytes. v2 splits content into more, array-shaped attributes, so this path gets more likely after migration, not less. Trap 5: exclude-newer-span in uv.lock blocked the new version Not schema-related, but it happened in the same change. Dependabot's ADK 2.13 PR was failing CI. Trying to reproduce locally, I could not even install 2.13: Because only google-adk<=2.12.0 is available ... The cause lives at the top of uv.lock : exclude-newer = "0001-01-01T00:00:00Z" exclude-newer-span = "P1W" exclude-newer-span refuses anything published within a week of the lock's resolution timestamp — a reasonable supply-chain measure. In this case 2.13.0 was published about five and a half hours past the cutoff. A few hours of timing, and the error message tells you none of this. Worse, my own ~/.config/uv/uv.toml carried exclude-newer = "1 week" , which overrode the PR's lockfile. That is why checking out the branch and running uv sync kept installing 2.7.0. # A stale VIRTUAL_ENV will also make `uv pip list` lie to you unset VIRTUAL_ENV UV_EXCLUDE_NEWER = 2026-12-31T00:00:00Z uv sync Reproducibility settings manufacture exactly as much irreproducibility for anyone who did not write them, because the failure never points back at the setting. Trap 6: a sys.modules stub leaking across test files The Dependabot CI failure turned out to have nothing to do with production code. Excluding one broken test file, all 1,243 remaining tests passed. Two independent causes, both test scaffolding. First, a test module installed stubs into sys.modules at import time and never cleaned up: # tests/test_leaf_agent.py google_genai_types = types . ModuleType ( " google.genai.types " ) google_genai_types . GenerateContentConfig = MagicMock ( name = " GenerateContentConfig " ) sys . modules [ " google.genai " ] = google_genai sys . modules [ " google.genai.types " ] = google_genai_types _MCP_CLIENT_STUB = _build_stub_modules () # runs at import, no teardown sys.modules is process-global. Depending on collection order, another test file imports google.genai.types , gets the stub, and dies with ImportError during collection. It happened to work on ADK 2.7 and broke on 2.13 when the import path changed. Second, contents.types no longer exists in ADK 2.13: original_contents_types = contents . types # AttributeError on ADK 2.13 The nasty part: a plain python -c import succeeds. It only fails under pytest, because only pytest collects the other module that plants the stub. I lost a good while to "the import works but CI fails." If an import error will not reproduce outside pytest, suspect sys.modules pollution first. Bonus: an all-NULL column is not evidence of zero While verifying the migration I noticed a new ADK 2.13 warning: App "router" can transfer between agents but has no context_cache_config. Every transfer swaps the system instruction and the tool set, so the request prefix changes and the whole prompt is re-sent uncached after each transfer. So I went to measure how much caching was actually happening: JSON_VALUE ( attributes , '$."gen_ai.usage.cached_input_tokens"' ) AS cached_tok All NULL. I concluded caching had never once engaged, and filed an issue saying so. That was wrong. The real attribute is gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens . The key I queried does not exist at all: # google/adk/telemetry/_token_usage.py GEN_AI_USAGE_CACHE_READ_INPUT_TOKENS = ' gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens ' GEN_AI_USAGE_CACHE_CREATION_INPUT_TOKENS = ' gen_ai.usage.cache_creation.input_tokens ' Re-run with the right key, and caching had been working before the fix: Time Agent input_tokens cache_read.input_tokens 10-31 07:41 leaf_agent 19,290 — 10-31 07:41 leaf_agent 23,599 — 10-31 07:41 leaf_agent 24,472 19,410 10-31 07:41 leaf_agent 26,465 23,359 Vertex AI's implicit caching was already kicking in from the third call. My premise of "zero caching" never held. What makes this trap sharp is that ADK sets usage attributes conditionally : if self . cache_read_input_tokens is not None : attrs [ GEN_AI_USAGE_CACHE_READ_INPUT_TOKENS ] = self . cache_read_input_tokens When the value is None , the attribute is absent entirely. So a NULL from a JSON path means "the value was zero", or "you typed the key wrong", or "this span never carries that attribute" — three very different things that look identical. The cheap guard is to check whether the attribute exists on any row before drawing a conclusion: SELECT COUNTIF ( JSON_VALUE ( attributes , '$."gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens"' ) IS NOT NULL ) AS has_attr , COUNT ( * ) AS n FROM spans WHERE name LIKE 'generate_content%' If has_attr = 0 , suspect the key before you suspect reality. The context_cache_config fix was still worth doing — explicit caching genuinely was unset. After enabling it: Time Agent input_tokens cache_read.input_tokens 11-01 08:05 router 2,875 — 11-01 08:06 router 3,010 — 11-01 08:06 leaf_agent 19,410 — 11-01 08:06 leaf_agent 23,655 19,391 11-01 08:06 leaf_agent 24,554 19,391 11-01 08:06 leaf_agent 24,757 19,391 11-01 08:07 leaf_agent 24,958 19,391 Hit rate improved (2/4 to 4/5), but the honest description is "the implicit caching that already existed became more consistent", not "caching started working". The router agent never caches, by design. Per ContextCacheConfig 's docstring, a cacheable prefix needs 2,048 tokens on Gemini 2.5 and 4,096 on Gemini 3 ; the router's 2,875–3,010 tokens never reach it. Agents with small instructions stay outside explicit caching no matter what you configure. Takeaways Schema v2 changes span names and attribute keys. Nothing errors — you just get zero rows. Capture real spans and diff them before you migrate queries. Set OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT , or no content is recorded. For trace-only setups, SPAN_ONLY . v1 and v2 LLM bodies live on different rows, so COALESCE cannot bridge them. Tool arguments and results share a row, so there it works. The 64 KiB attribute limit kills the whole batch. SDK character truncation corrupts JSON; shrink with structural knowledge. exclude-newer-span produces failures whose cause is unreadable from the error. Tests that plant stubs in sys.modules must tear them down. Classic symptom: an import error that will not reproduce under python -c . Never read an all-NULL column as proof that something did not happen. Wrong key names and conditionally-set attributes look exactly the same. For version deltas, google-adk on PyPI and the adk-python releases are the fastest reference. For attribute names, read the semconv constants directly rather than any blog post — including this one. I got them wrong twice.

title: I wanted to 3D-print a fox an AI made from one picture. The fix was to stop looking for its surface
author: Helgard
summary: Image-to-3D models are good now. You give Idol one picture of a toy fox, and about a minute later you can spin a 3D fox in your browser, including the back it never saw. Then you try to print it, and you hit a wall: the model did not make a mesh. It made a Gaussian splat , a cloud of soft, semi-transparent blobs. Slicers want a closed surface, and a cloud of blobs has none. This post is about getting from that cloud to a clean, watertight STL. The method that worked is old and simple. Getting to it took four failed attempts, and the failures are the useful part. Code: https://github.com/helgard-orlm/splat2stl . It converts a splat in 8–16 seconds on an 8 GB RTX 5060 with one command. Who did what, up front: I set the goal, judged every result in a slicer, and made the two calls that mattered: "your first version was almost perfect, everything after it is worse" and "why not photograph the fox from all sides, like photogrammetry apps do". The code and the experiments were done by Claude (Anthropic) in my sessions. GLM-5.3 acted as a second opinion: it found the wrong assumption behind the failed attempts and reviewed the README before release. "We" below means the three of us. What a splat is, in one paragraph A splat stores a few hundred thousand ellipsoid blobs. Each blob has a position, a size, a rotation, a color and an opacity. A viewer draws them front to back and blends them, the way layers of tinted glass add up. There is no lighting step: the colors already contain the shading, including any glossy highlights that were in the input picture. The obvious approaches, and why they failed Every textbook route from points to a surface has the same shape: decide where the surface is, then wrap triangles around it. So we tried to find the surface. Threshold the blobs. Treat every blob above some opacity as solid and wrap it. The fox came out with bumps on its head and face that you could not see in the browser. Find the depth where the fox becomes opaque. From 60 directions, march through the blobs and mark the point where accumulated opacity crosses 50%. The head came out pitted, "as if eaten by acid", in my words at the time. Average depth plus Poisson reconstruction. Take the viewer's average depth from many directions as a point cloud, then let screened Poisson (the algorithm behind MeshLab's reconstruction filter) stretch a smooth skin over it. The head came out grainy. Blur the opacity and take one iso-surface. Smooth by construction, or so we thought. The face came out swollen and covered in bubbles. The body and the tail were fine in every attempt. Only the head kept failing. Halfway through, we finally printed some statistics about the head, and they already held the answer. It took two more attempts and a second opinion to accept it. The head is fog On the body, the median blob opacity is 0.85 , and 67% of the blobs are more than half opaque. On the head, the median opacity is 0.01 , and only 4% are more than half opaque. Idol built the head out of tens of thousands of almost transparent blobs stacked in layers. In the viewer, these layers add up to a smooth, solid-looking head. Across the whole fox, 51% of the blobs have opacity below 0.1. We generated the same fox with three other random seeds and got 47%, 51% and 54%, so this is how the model sees this picture, not bad luck. A stone house or a pirate ship from the same model was only 3–7% fog, which is why the methods worked on them. That explained all four failures at once, and GLM put it bluntly: inside fog there is no surface to find. Where the fog "becomes solid" depends on the direction you look from. Every method that searches for that place turns the disagreement between directions into artifacts: bumps, pits, grain or bubbles. The four attempts were not four bugs. They were one wrong assumption. Stop looking for the surface. Use the outline Here is the thing that is well defined even for fog: the outline. Look at the fox from any direction, and the opacity accumulated through the whole head is high, so its silhouette is crisp. My first version had already used silhouettes, which is why it was "almost perfect". Its glitches came from building those silhouettes out of individual blobs with a low threshold, so stray wisps of fog poked out as small bumps. The fix was to take the outline from real pictures of the splat, exactly as the browser shows it: Photograph it. We wrote a small splat renderer in plain PyTorch (no CUDA extension to compile). It draws each blob as a soft ellipse and blends the layers front to back, like the browser does. It takes about 140 pictures from directions spread over a sphere, from the top down to 60° below the horizon. Take the outline in each picture : every pixel where the accumulated opacity is above 50%. Carve like a sculptor. Start with a block of 256³ voxels. A voxel survives only if it falls inside the outline in every picture. What remains looks like the fox from every direction, and it is solid inside. Skin and color. Marching cubes turns the voxels into triangles, light smoothing removes the voxel steps, and each vertex takes its color from the picture that sees it most head-on. This is the classic visual hull , known since the 1990s ( Laurentini, 1994 ). Nothing here is a new algorithm. What is specific is where the outline comes from: from properly blended renders of the splat, not from the blobs themselves. That is the difference between fog becoming bumps and fog becoming a smooth head. We also tried real photogrammetry on those pictures (COLMAP's patch-match stereo with the known cameras). Its depth was accurate where it found texture, about 0.35 mm at a print height of 80 mm, but it found texture on only about half of the fox. Using it to carve concavities roughened the smooth plastic, so it is not part of the tool. Its real value was proving that clean pictures were the key. Results We tested twelve objects: eleven generated by Idol and one pirate ship generated by TripoSplat, another image-to-3D model. All twelve meshes are watertight, and each took 8–16 seconds. The converter needs about 2.4 GB of GPU memory. The limitations are the classic ones for this method, and you can see them in the picture: Hidden hollows are filled. If no direction can see into a hollow, the outline cannot carve it. The seat of the bowl-shaped papasan chair is filled flat, and so is the inside of the watering can. Handles and arches survive, because you can see through them from the side. Very thin parts disappear. Anything thinner than about two voxels (≈0.6 mm on an 80 mm print) is lost to smoothing: ship rigging, the thin rattan stand of the papasan chair. Highlights are baked into the colors. The fox was glossy in the input picture, so the colored OBJ has light patches on its head. The STL geometry is unaffected. The clean fix is to make the input picture matte before generating. Try it git clone https://github.com/helgard-orlm/splat2stl && cd splat2stl pip install -e . python -m splat2stl fox.ply out/fox --height 80 # out/fox.stl (Z up, millimetres) and out/fox_color.obj (vertex colors) It expects a splat of a single object. --up sets the up axis ( -y by default, which matches Idol, TripoSplat and most 3DGS generators). --smooth (0–5) trades detail for smoothness. What I took away Look at the data before tuning the method, and believe it. Two variants of "find the depth" went by before anyone printed the opacity statistics of the head. Even after the numbers said "fog", we spent two more attempts searching that fog for a surface. One table explained everything; it just had to be taken seriously. When the first version is "almost right", fix its specific glitches. Each new attempt replaced the whole approach and threw away what was working. The final tool is version one with its silhouettes taken from proper renders. Measure what is well defined, not what you wish you had. Depth inside fog does not exist. The outline does. Building on the outline gave a solid that is closed by construction, which is exactly what a printer needs. Credits: 3D Gaussian Splatting by Kerbl et al. (SIGGRAPH 2023); visual hull by Laurentini (1994); test objects generated with Idol (Apache-2.0) and TripoSplat (MIT). Other splat-to-mesh tools worth knowing: 3DGS-to-PC and NVIDIA's fVDB . They recover hollows on clean, opaque splats, which a silhouette method cannot do.

title: The 18 FEC columns and the 10 errors that fail a French tax audit
author: Vincent
summary: Every French company that keeps its books on a computer must be able to hand the tax administration one file: the FEC , Fichier des Écritures Comptables . Accounting software exports it in one click, so everyone assumes it is correct. It often isn't. A FEC that is late or does not follow the required format costs a €5,000 fine under article 1729 D of the French tax code (CGI). For a remote audit ( examen de comptabilité ), the administration's own guidance, updated in January 2026, applies it once per audit (BOI-CF-DG-40-20 § 390). Worse than the fine, a file the auditor cannot read is a bad start to an audit. This guide lists the 18 columns, then ten errors I see in real exports, each with a bad line, why it fails and the fix. Every example below comes from synthetic files and from the output of two checkers I wrote; the rules are checked against the official text. What a FEC is Since 2014, a company under audit must hand over its accounting entries as a file at the start of the audit (article L47 A of the Livre des procédures fiscales , LPF). For a remote audit, it has 15 days from the notice. The format is fixed by article A47 A-1 LPF and explained in the administration's guidance BOI-CF-IOR-60-40-20. The file holds every entry recorded during the fiscal year, opening balances included, one line per entry line. Most companies send a flat text file; an XML format also exists, but this guide covers the flat file. The 18 columns For a company taxed on commercial profits (BIC or corporate tax), the file has exactly these 18 columns, in this order . Cash-basis non-commercial and agricultural filers add columns (22 and 21); they are out of scope here. # Column Content Example 1 JournalCode Journal code VE 2 JournalLib Journal name Ventes 3 EcritureNum Entry number, on a continuous sequence 000039 4 EcritureDate Accounting date, AAAAMMJJ 20250610 5 CompteNum Account number 411000 6 CompteLib Account name Clients 7 CompAuxNum Sub-ledger account (customer, supplier); may be empty CLI001 8 CompAuxLib Sub-ledger account name; filled when 7 is Atelier Durand 9 PieceRef Supporting document reference F2025-06 10 PieceDate Document date, AAAAMMJJ 20250610 11 EcritureLib Entry label Facture F2025-06 Atelier Durand 12 Debit Debit amount, decimal comma 3960,00 13 Credit Credit amount, decimal comma 0,00 14 EcritureLet Matching (lettrage) code; may be empty AA 15 DateLet Matching date; filled when 14 is 20250712 16 ValidDate Date the entry was validated 20250610 17 Montantdevise Amount in foreign currency; may be empty 1200,00 18 Idevise Currency code; filled when 17 is USD A full line looks like this (pipe-separated): VE|Ventes|000039|20250610|411000|Clients|CLI001|Atelier Durand|F2025-06|20250610|Facture F2025-06 Atelier Durand|3960,00|0,00|||20250610|| If your software has no separate debit and credit, the text allows Montant and Sens (D/C or +1/-1) instead of columns 12 and 13. Most exports use Debit/Credit. The 10 errors 1. Wrong file name FEC_2025.txt Why it fails: the name is part of the format: the company's SIREN, the letters FEC , then the fiscal year's closing date as AAAAMMJJ (A47 A-1, IX). Fix: 123456782FEC20251231.txt for SIREN 123456782 and a year closing on 31 December 2025. The text fixes the name, not the extension; .txt is the usual choice for the flat file. Also check that the SIREN is right: it has a Luhn check digit, so a typo is often detectable. 2. Mixed or wrong separator VE|Ventes|000002|20250310|411000|Clients|||F000002|20250310|Facture F1|120,00|0,00|||20250310|| VE;Ventes;000002;20250310;706000;Prestations;;;F000002;20250310;Facture F1;0,00;120,00;;;20250310;; Why it fails: fields are separated by a tab or a pipe ( | ), the same one for the whole file (A47 A-1, VI). Semicolons, the default of many spreadsheets in France, are not allowed. The second line above has 1 field instead of 18 for a pipe reader, so the checker reports field_count on line 5, and the entry then looks unbalanced because half of it cannot be read. Fix: export the FEC from the accounting software, never through a spreadsheet. If you must edit it, save as "text (tab-separated)" and check that no label contains the separator. 3. Broken accents VE|Ventes|000002|20250310|411000|Clients|||F000002|20250310|Facture rÃ©glÃ©e|120,00|0,00|||20250310|| Why it fails: the allowed encodings are ASCII, ISO 8859-15 and UTF-8 (A47 A-1, XII). rÃ©glÃ©e is "réglée" encoded twice: someone opened a UTF-8 file as Latin-1 and saved it as UTF-8 again. The labels are now wrong in the copy the auditor reads. Fix: pick one encoding and never re-save the file in a text editor or spreadsheet. A file in UTF-16 ("Unicode text" in Excel) is outside the list too: re-export it as UTF-8. Be aware: no automatic check can be sure here. A double-encoded label is still valid UTF-8, so both tools below accept it. Search the file for Ã before sending it. 4. Misspelled or reordered headers JournalCode|JournalLib|EcritureNum|DateEcriture|CompteNum|CompteLib|CompAuxNum|CompAuxLib|PieceRef|PieceDate|EcritureLib|Credit|Debit|EcritureLet|DateLet|ValidDate|Montantdevise Why it fails: three problems in one line. DateEcriture instead of EcritureDate , Credit before Debit , and Idevise missing. The checker reports: error header_count x1: The header must contain exactly 18 columns. error header_missing x2: Mandatory column missing from the header: EcritureDate. error header_unknown x1: Header column not defined by article A47 A-1. error header_order x1: The header columns are not in the required order. Fix: copy the header from the table above, exactly, case included. Empty optional columns stay in the header. 5. Dates not in AAAAMMJJ AC|Achats|000009|20250230|613200|Locations immobilieres|||FL02|20250205|Facture FL02 SCI Les Tilleuls|1200,00|0,00|||20250205|| AC|Achats|000026|12/04/2025|626000|Frais postaux et telecom|||FT04|20250411|Facture FT04 Telecom Ouest|89,90|0,00|||20250411|| Why it fails: dates are AAAAMMJJ with no separator (A47 A-1, XII). 12/04/2025 has the wrong format. 20250230 has the right format but does not exist (there is no 30 February), which a format check alone misses: error date_invalid x3: Non-existent date in EcritureDate. - line(s) 21, 22, 23 error date_format x3: Wrong date format in EcritureDate (expected AAAAMMJJ). - line(s) 64, 65, 66 Fix: set the export's date format in the software. A non-existent date usually comes from a manual entry: correct the entry, then export again. 6. Decimal point or thousands separators in amounts VE|Ventes|000002|20250310|411000|Clients|||F000002|20250310|Facture F1|120.00|0,00|||20250310|| VE|Ventes|000002|20250310|411000|Clients|||F000002|20250310|Facture F1|1 200,00|0,00|||20250310|| Why it fails: the comma separates units from decimals, and no thousands separator is accepted (A47 A-1, XII). 120.00 and 1 200,00 both fail. Fix: 120,00 and 1200,00 . One detail people get wrong in the other direction: a negative amount may carry its sign as the first character on the left or the last on the right ( -150,00 or 150,00- ), both are legal. 7. Unbalanced entries VE|Ventes|000039|20250610|411000|Clients|CLI001|Atelier Durand|F2025-06|20250610|Facture F2025-06 Atelier Durand|3960,00|0,00|||20250610|| VE|Ventes|000039|20250610|706000|Prestations de services|||F2025-06|20250610|Facture F2025-06 Atelier Durand|0,00|3200,00|||20250610|| VE|Ventes|000039|20250610|445710|TVA collectee|||F2025-06|20250610|Facture F2025-06 Atelier Durand|0,00|660,00|||20250610|| Why it fails: double-entry bookkeeping. The lines of one entry (same EcritureNum ) must have total debit = total credit, and so must the whole file. Here 3960,00 debit against 3860,00 credit: error entry_unbalanced x1: Unbalanced entry: debit - credit difference of 100,00. error file_unbalanced x1: The file is unbalanced: total debit 193104,48, total credit 193004,48, difference 100,00. Fix: software does not book unbalanced entries, so this almost always means the export lost or changed lines: a filter on accounts, a truncated label that shifted a column, or a manual edit. Find the entry by its number and compare with the ledger. 8. Gaps or duplicates in EcritureNum AC|Achats|000046|20250704|401000|Fournisseurs|FOU002|SCI Les Tilleuls|FL07|20250704|Facture FL07 SCI Les Tilleuls|0,00|1440,00|||20250704|| VE|Ventes|000050|20250710|411000|Clients|CLI002|Boulangerie Martin|F2025-07|20250710|Facture F2025-07 Boulangerie Martin|4140,00|0,00|||20250710|| Why it fails: EcritureNum is "the number on a continuous sequence" (A47 A-1, VII). Entries 47 to 49 are missing, which is exactly what an auditor looks for: deleted entries. error num_gap x1: Numbering gap: 3 number(s) missing, from 47 to 49. The sequence can be global or per journal ( VE0001 , AC0001 …); a checker has to work out which one the file uses before counting gaps. The same number used twice for two different entries is the opposite error. Fix: if entries were really deleted, the file shows it and you need an explanation. More often, the export left out a journal or a period: export the whole fiscal year, all journals. 9. Missing ValidDate or validation out of order VE|Ventes|000002|20250310|411000|Clients|||F000002|20250310|Facture F1|120,00|0,00||||| Why it fails: ValidDate is the date the entry became final and can no longer be changed. The file is sorted in chronological order of validation (A47 A-1, VII), so an empty ValidDate means a draft entry was exported. Dates going backwards against the numbering are a red flag too: error validdate_not_chronological x1: Validation date earlier than that of entry no. 71 (20251020): validation must follow numbering order. Fix: validate (close) the draft entries for the year in the software, then export again. 10. Opening entries missing or misplaced VE|Ventes|000001|20250310|411000|Clients|||F000001|20250310|Facture F1|120,00|0,00|||20250310|| VE|Ventes|000001|20250310|706000|Prestations|||F000001|20250310|Facture F1|0,00|120,00|||20250310|| AN|A-nouveaux|000002|20250101|512000|Banque|||AN2025|20250101|Reprise des soldes|15000,00|0,00|||20250315|| AN|A-nouveaux|000002|20250101|101000|Capital|||AN2025|20250101|Reprise des soldes|0,00|15000,00|||20250315|| Why it fails: the file must include the entries that record the opening balance sheet ( à-nouveaux ), and they normally take the first entry numbers of the year (A47 A-1, VII). The administration accepts them later in the file only if they cannot come first and the auditor can still identify them (BOI-CF-IOR-60-40-20). A file with no opening entries at all does not let the auditor check the balances. Fix: include the opening journal (usually AN ) in the export and number it first. Be aware: I know of no automatic checker, including mine, that verifies this today; check it by eye in the first lines of the file. A 20-line header check in Python The header causes a large share of rejections and is the easiest thing to check. This is the header logic of fec-lint , reduced to plain Python with no dependency: EXPECTED = [ ' JournalCode ' , ' JournalLib ' , ' EcritureNum ' , ' EcritureDate ' , ' CompteNum ' , ' CompteLib ' , ' CompAuxNum ' , ' CompAuxLib ' , ' PieceRef ' , ' PieceDate ' , ' EcritureLib ' , ' Debit ' , ' Credit ' , ' EcritureLet ' , ' DateLet ' , ' ValidDate ' , ' Montantdevise ' , ' Idevise ' ] def check_header ( path , encoding = ' utf-8 ' ): with open ( path , encoding = encoding ) as f : header = f . readline (). lstrip ( ' ﻿ ' ). rstrip ( ' \r\n ' ) sep = ' \t ' if ' \t ' in header else ' | ' if ' | ' in header else None if sep is None : return [ ' no tab or pipe separator in the header ' ] names = [ n . strip () for n in header . split ( sep )] errors = [] if len ( names ) != 18 : errors . append ( f ' { len ( names ) } columns instead of 18 ' ) errors += [ f ' missing column: { n } ' for n in EXPECTED if n not in names ] errors += [ f ' unknown column: { n } ' for n in names if n not in EXPECTED ] found = [ n for n in names if n in EXPECTED ] if found != [ n for n in EXPECTED if n in found ]: errors . append ( ' columns are not in the required order ' ) return errors On the header from error 4 it returns: 17 columns instead of 18 missing column: EcritureDate missing column: Idevise unknown column: DateEcriture columns are not in the required order Two details matter. The order check compares only the columns that were found, so a missing column does not hide a swap. And lstrip('﻿') removes the byte-order mark some Windows tools add, which would otherwise make the first column ﻿JournalCode . How to check your own file Test Compta Demat , the administration's free tool, checks the file the way the DGFiP reads it. Start there; it is the reference. fec-lint , free and open source (MIT): errors 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6, a UTF-16 file for error 3 and an empty ValidDate for error 9, as a command line tool and an MCP server for AI assistants. It runs on your machine and the file never leaves it. pipx install fec-lint fec-lint 123456782FEC20251231.txt FEC Checker , the full pre-audit: everything above plus balance, numbering, validation order, risk signals (weekend postings, round amounts, Benford's law, cash and suspense accounts) and an optional AI-written fix list, in French or English: FEC Checker on Apify . None of these replaces reading the first and last lines of the file yourself, especially for errors 3 and 10. Technical guide, not tax advice. It describes the published file format; it does not tell you how the administration will judge your accounts. For that, ask your accountant (expert-comptable).

title: LLM-as-Judge Position Bias: Swapping A/B Flipped 87 of 300 Verdicts
author: jidonglab
summary: In a head-to-head eval, my new system prompt beat the old one in 66% of comparisons. I already had the "we're shipping v2" message typed. Then I swapped which answer went first and reran the exact same 300 pairs. The new prompt won 43%. The judge, the answers, the rubric and temperature 0 were all the same. The only change was which answer sat in the slot labeled "A". That is LLM-as-judge position bias , and if your eval script calls judge(new, old) in a fixed order, your headline number is probably measuring it too. TL;DR LLM-as-judge position bias means a pairwise judge prefers whichever answer sits in a particular slot (usually the first) regardless of quality. In my run, swapping A and B flipped 87 of 300 verdicts (29%) , and 78 of those flips went to whichever answer was in slot A. The bias shows up in close calls. When two answers are near-equal, slot position acts as the tiebreaker. Fix: judge every pair in both orders . Count a win only when both runs agree, and treat disagreement as a tie. Before trusting a judge, run the mirror test : put the identical answer in both slots. A fair judge has no reason to prefer either one. What is LLM-as-judge position bias? LLM-as-judge position bias is a judge model's tendency to pick an answer because of where it appears in the prompt, not because of what it says. It's one of the first biases documented for LLM judges (the MT-Bench / Chatbot Arena paper from Zheng et al. called it out back in 2023), and it's still easy to walk straight into. It hits pairwise evals hardest, the "here are Answer A and Answer B, which is better?" setup. That's the setup most of us use to compare prompts, models or RAG configs, because it's easier than defining an absolute 1-10 scale. How I caught it My eval script looked like every eval script: for q in questions : verdict = ask_judge ( q . text , new_answer [ q . id ], old_answer [ q . id ]) wins += verdict == " A " The new answer always went in slot A. I didn't pick that order for any reason. It was just the order of the function arguments. A coworker asked "did you swap them?" and I had no good answer. So I ran it again with the old answer in slot A. Here is what the 300 pairs did across both runs: Outcome across both orders Pairs New prompt won both times 120 Old prompt won both times 93 Slot A won both times (verdict flipped) 78 Slot B won both times (verdict flipped) 9 Count the slot picks: slot A won 369 of 600 judgments, or 61.5%. A judge with no position preference would land somewhere near 50%. The 66% headline was really 120 consistent wins plus 78 pairs where the new prompt just happened to sit in the favored seat. Why does an LLM judge prefer the first answer? An LLM judge prefers the first answer mostly because of how it reads: one token at a time, left to right. Answer A gets evaluated with nothing to compare it to. By the time the model reaches Answer B, it has already formed a picture of what "good" looks like for this question, and that picture came from A. A few things stack on top of that: Close calls get decided by the seat. I read the 87 flipped pairs myself. In most of them I couldn't pick a winner either: both answers were correct, worded differently, and about the same length. With no real quality signal to go on, the position prior decides. Temperature 0 doesn't help. It makes the bias reproducible, which is worse in a way, because rerunning the same order gives you the same wrong answer and feels like confirmation. The direction isn't universal. Some judge and prompt combinations favor slot B, especially with long answers where the most recent text is freshest. My judge favored A. Yours might favor B. Measure it before you assume a direction. Format priors. "A" is the first option in countless multiple-choice examples the model has seen. Label tokens carry their own baggage before the model reads a word of the answers. None of this means the judge is useless. On the 213 pairs where it agreed with itself, its picks matched mine on almost every one I spot-checked. The judge is fine at clear differences. On near-ties it isn't measuring quality at all. How do you test an LLM judge for position bias? Run the mirror test: build pairs where Answer A and Answer B are the exact same text, then ask the judge to pick. A fair judge has no basis to prefer either, so it should say TIE or split close to 50/50. I ran 50 mirror pairs. My judge picked A 34 times, B 9 times and TIE 7 times. It was confidently picking a winner between two copies of the same text, and it usually picked the first one. This takes ten minutes and tells you more about your judge than a week of reading verdicts. I now run it every time I change the judge model or the judge prompt. How do you fix position bias in pairwise LLM evals? Judge every pair twice, once in each order, and count a win only when both runs agree. If the judge contradicts itself, call it a tie. That's the whole fix: JUDGE_PROMPT = """ You are comparing two answers to the same question. Question: {question} Answer A: {a} Answer B: {b} Briefly list the strengths and weaknesses of each answer. Then end with exactly one line: VERDICT: A, VERDICT: B, or VERDICT: TIE """ def ask_judge ( question , a , b ): out = call_llm ( JUDGE_PROMPT . format ( question = question , a = a , b = b ), temperature = 0 ) return parse_verdict ( out ) # "A" | "B" | "TIE" def judge_pair ( question , new , old ): run1 = ask_judge ( question , new , old ) # new in slot A run2 = ask_judge ( question , old , new ) # new in slot B if run1 == " A " and run2 == " B " : return " new " if run1 == " B " and run2 == " A " : return " old " # Self-contradiction, or a TIE in either run: no signal. return " tie " Then report three numbers instead of one: results = [ judge_pair ( q . text , new [ q . id ], old [ q . id ]) for q in questions ] n = len ( results ) new_wins = results . count ( " new " ) old_wins = results . count ( " old " ) ties = results . count ( " tie " ) print ( f " new { new_wins / n : . 0 % } old { old_wins / n : . 0 % } tie { ties / n : . 0 % } " ) print ( f " new win rate on decisive pairs: { new_wins / ( new_wins + old_wins ) : . 0 % } " ) The tie rate is the important number here. It tells you how much of your eval set the judge can't actually separate. If it's 30%, a 5-point swing in your headline doesn't mean much. Some other things that helped: Give the judge a TIE option. Without it, you're forcing a coin flip on every near-equal pair, and the position prior is what decides the flip. Ask for reasoning before the verdict. Put the verdict line last so the model writes its comparison before it commits to a letter. It doesn't remove the bias, but it cut my flip rate. Use logprobs if your API exposes them. Take P("A") in one order and P("B") in the swapped order, then average. You get a soft score that's symmetric by construction. Isn't randomizing the A/B order enough? Randomizing the order per pair is better than a fixed order, but it doesn't fix the problem. Random assignment spreads the position bias evenly across both systems, so your aggregate win rate stops being skewed in one direction. That's real progress. What it hides is the noise. Those 87 coin-flip pairs are still in your data, now split randomly between "new won" and "old won." Your headline drifts toward 50% and looks like an honest close race, when actually a third of your eval set says nothing at all. Rerun it with a different random seed and the number moves. Running both orders costs twice the judge calls. On 300 pairs, that's 300 extra API calls. Shipping a prompt that was never better costs more. Which other LLM judge biases show up alongside position bias? Position bias rarely travels alone. Watch for these two: Verbosity bias. Judges tend to favor the longer answer, even when the extra length is padding. If your new prompt makes answers 40% longer, some of its "wins" are word count. Check the win rate split by length difference. Self-preference. A judge can favor outputs that sound like its own writing. If you're comparing Model X against Model Y and Model X is also the judge, be suspicious of a big X win. Swapping the order fixes neither of these. They need their own checks. So was my new prompt actually better? Yes, a little. On the 213 pairs where the judge agreed with itself, the new prompt won 120 to 93, which is 56%. That's a real but modest improvement. It isn't the 66% blowout I nearly announced. I shipped it with a much quieter message and a note that 29% of the eval set was a toss-up. How does LLM-as-judge position bias distort pairwise evals? LLM-as-judge position bias makes a pairwise judge favor whichever answer occupies a particular slot, usually the first. It mostly decides near-tie comparisons, which can quietly inflate or deflate a win rate by double digits. In my eval, swapping A and B flipped 87 of 300 verdicts and turned a 66% win into 43%. The fix is to judge every pair in both orders, count only verdicts that agree, treat contradictions as ties, and report the tie rate next to the win rate. Run the mirror test, with the identical answer in both slots, before you trust any judge. Written by the developer behind Preterview , an interview prep platform.

title: Python: checar preço de produto passando por proxy residencial (e calcular o custo por página)
author: Nuvem Dev
summary: Quando o scraping começa a tomar bloqueio, o culpado costuma ser o IP do seu servidor. Aqui vai um script curto que passa a requisição por um proxy (se você tiver um) e já estima quanto aquela página custou em tráfego. Eu rodei esse script de verdade contra um servidor local, sem proxy, só pra validar o código. Não testei com um proxy pago nesta edição. 1. Instala pip install requests 2. O script import os , sys , requests # PROXY_URL no formato http://usuario:senha@host:porta (vem do painel do provedor) proxy = os . getenv ( " PROXY_URL " ) proxies = { " http " : proxy , " https " : proxy } if proxy else None def pega ( url ): r = requests . get ( url , proxies = proxies , timeout = 15 , headers = { " User-Agent " : " Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; checa-preco/0.1) " }) r . raise_for_status () return r if __name__ == " __main__ " : url = sys . argv [ 1 ] r = pega ( url ) kb = len ( r . content ) / 1024 print ( f " status= { r . status_code } tamanho= { kb : . 1 f } KB via_proxy= { bool ( proxy ) } " ) print ( f " custo estimado a US$ 5,51/GB: US$ { kb / 1024 / 1024 * 5.51 : . 6 f } " ) 3. Rodando Sem proxy (testei assim, com uma página local): python checa_preco.py http://localhost:8765/index.html # status=200 tamanho=0.0 KB via_proxy=False Com proxy, é só exportar a variável antes: export PROXY_URL = "http://usuario:senha@host:porta" python checa_preco.py https://exemplo.com.br/produto Por que o custo por página importa Proxy residencial é cobrado por giga de tráfego. Na página oficial do IPRoyal (01/11/2026) o preço vai de US$ 7,35/GB no pacote de 1 GB a US$ 5,51/GB no de 10 GB, e o tráfego não expira. Uma página de 200 KB custa na casa de US$ 0,001. O que pesa mesmo é imagem e JavaScript: se der pra pedir só o HTML, o custo cai bastante. Boas práticas Leia os termos do site e o robots.txt antes de coletar. Se existir API oficial, use a API. Coloque um sleep entre requisições. Rotacionar IP não justifica martelar o servidor dos outros. Preços e planos do IPRoyal: https://go.nowto.link/iproyal Se curtiu, a versão newsletter com os números dos pacotes está na Substack: https://nuvemdev.substack.com . E o tutorial anterior (isolamento de perfil com Playwright) está no meu perfil: https://dev.to/nuvemdev Divulgação: alguns links são de afiliado. Se você comprar, eu posso ganhar uma comissão, sem custo extra pra você.

title: Our desktop app has to tell us which price it showed, and a build that cannot is charged £20 instead of €24.99
author: Daniel Pertu
summary: Notifio is a desktop app that watches rental search pages for new listings, sold as a one-time licence. The licence is £20 and the auto-reply upgrade is another £20, and those two numbers are the only prices in the codebase: export const PRICE_CURRENCY = " gbp " ; export const LICENSE_PRICE_PENCE = 2000 ; export const UPGRADE_PRICE_PENCE = 2000 ; Everything else a visitor sees is derived. A visitor in Ireland reads €24.99 on the pricing page and is charged €24.99, in euros, by Stripe. Not "about €24", not £20 converted at checkout time by Stripe's Adaptive Pricing, but the same integer the page rendered. That is one function and a table of 24 currencies, which I have written about from the Stripe side before . This post is about the one client in the system that cannot work its own price out, which is our own app, and what that forced into the API. How the figure is decided export function localPrice ( pence : number , currency : DisplayCurrency ): number { if ( pence === 0 ) return 0 ; if ( currency === BASE_CURRENCY ) return Math . round ( pence ); const digits = minorUnitDigits ( currency ); const major = ( pence / 100 ) * CURRENCIES [ currency ]. rate * LOCAL_PRICE_MARGIN ; return Math . round ( ceilToRetail ( major , digits ) * Math . pow ( 10 , digits )); } The rate is fixed in the table, taken from the ECB euro reference rates of a particular day and crossed through the euro. LOCAL_PRICE_MARGIN is 1.04, which covers Stripe's fee for converting the payout back into pounds and drift in those fixed rates. ceilToRetail rounds up to the next .99 , or the next whole unit in a currency written without decimals. Run £20 through it: Currency Shown and charged £20 at the table's own rate EUR €24.99 23.39 USD $28.99 27.12 SEK 267,99 kr 257.33 PLN 104,99 zł 100.73 INR ₹2,696.99 2592.80 HUF 8805 Ft 8466.20 JPY ￥4,491 4317.80 The right-hand column is why the fixed rate is defensible: it is not a conversion and the site never calls it one. It is a price list, in 24 currencies, that happens to have been generated from one pound figure, and the rates are fixed precisely so the price of the same licence cannot change between one page load and the next. The last two rows are where Stripe gets interesting. Intl says the forint and the yen are written without decimals, and Stripe agrees about the yen only, so ¥4,491 is sent as 4491 and 8805 Ft as 880500 . That rescaling is one line, and it has its own post . On the website, nobody is asked The currency comes from the request, on the server, for both the page and the checkout: export async function getDisplayCurrency (): Promise < DisplayCurrency > { const headerList = await headers (); return currencyForVisitor ( headerList . get ( " x-vercel-ip-country " ), headerList . get ( " user-agent " )); } 58 country codes map to the 24 currencies, and anything unlisted gets GBP. The checkout route calls the same currencyForVisitor with the same two headers, so the browser never sends a currency and never gets to choose one. Three pages give up static rendering for this, because reading a request header makes them per-request: the homepage, the download page and the pricing page are all force-dynamic . Crawlers are pinned to GBP by a user-agent check, so the price Google indexes is the price in the page's own structured data rather than the currency of whichever datacentre fetched it. And on every session we create without Managed Payments, Adaptive Pricing is explicitly switched off: ...( managed ? { managed_payments : { enabled : true } } : { adaptive_pricing : { enabled : false } }), Adaptive Pricing is a good feature in general and the wrong feature here: it exists to convert a price into the buyer's currency, and our price is already in the buyer's currency. Leaving it on means Stripe gets a chance to show a different number on the Checkout page from the one on ours. EU sales go through Managed Payments, where Stripe rejects the field outright, and the fact that the price is already local is exactly what gives it nothing to do. The client that cannot read the headers The auto-reply upgrade is bought from inside the desktop app, because it needs the licence that is already on the machine. The app does not render our pages, so it cannot learn the visitor's country from a Vercel header on a page request. It learns the price from the licence check it already makes: const currency = currencyForVisitor ( countryFromRequest ( req ), req . headers . get ( " user-agent " )); return NextResponse . json ({ ... upgradePrice : priceQuote ( UPGRADE_PRICE_PENCE , currency ), }); priceQuote returns two fields: the currency, and the formatted label the app puts on the button. Then, when somebody clicks it, the app sends that currency back, and the upgrade route only accepts it if it agrees: let currency : DisplayCurrency = BASE_CURRENCY ; if ( shownCurrency !== undefined ) { const shown = typeof shownCurrency === " string " ? parseDisplayCurrency ( shownCurrency ) : null ; if ( shown !== localCurrency ) { return NextResponse . json ( { error : " The price for your country has been updated. Check it and try again. " , upgradePrice : priceQuote ( UPGRADE_PRICE_PENCE , localCurrency ), }, { status : 409 } ); } currency = localCurrency ; } This is the only client-supplied currency in the system, and it is not trusted, it is only allowed to confirm. The server works out the currency the same way it always does, and the client's value is a claim about what was on screen. If the two disagree, nobody is charged: the response carries the current price so the app can show it first. Quoting one figure and charging another is the single thing this whole module exists to prevent, and a mismatch is the one case where the app genuinely cannot know which figure is right. Three things I do not like about that block The 409 message describes the wrong cause. "The price for your country has been updated" is the rarest reason to get here. The common ones are a quote cached from a previous trip, a VPN that is on for one request and off for the next, and a mobile connection that moves the user between two geolocations. A user on a VPN can retry forever and get the same answer, because nothing in the app tells them the two requests are being seen from different countries. The response has room for both currencies, and the copy should say which one we think they are in. Nothing is logged. The 409 returns without a console.error , so the one failure in the purchase path that depends on something outside our code is invisible. One log line with the two currency codes in it would turn "a user says the upgrade button does nothing" into a two-minute answer. The compatibility branch is also an opt-out. shownCurrency !== undefined exists because app builds from before local prices send no currency and display a fixed £20, so charging them £20 is the honest thing to do. The consequence is that the field being absent selects the base price, and for all 23 non-GBP currencies the base price is the cheaper one by construction, since the local price is the conversion plus 4% rounded up. Anybody who removes one field from one request pays £20 instead of €24.99. The amount at stake is the FX margin on a £20 sale, so this is not a fraud problem, it is a correctness one: the same product has two prices and the client picks. The obvious fix is to accept a missing currency only from the builds that predate the feature, and I cannot write it, because the app never tells the server which version it is. Nothing in the licence check carries a version string, so the absence of the currency field is currently our only signal that we are talking to an older build, which is the same thing as having no signal at all. So the honest shape of the fix is a floor rather than a gate: never charge less than the local price, and let the quote be the only thing that decides which it is. And the version field is going in, because the app has no auto-update, those old builds will keep arriving for years, and right now the server cannot tell one from the other. What the tests pin The pricing and checkout rules are the one part of this codebase with real test coverage: 42 cases on the currency module, 14 on the session parameters, and 23 on the Managed Payments decision. The ones worth stealing are not the arithmetic ones. They are: Every EU-27 country is listed with its own currency, so no EU sale can reach Managed Payments with a currency Stripe would want to convert. localPrice never returns less than the same sale in GBP, for every currency in the table. Zero stays zero in all 24, because a retail round-up on a free tier would invent a price of €0.99 for something that costs nothing. That last one is my favourite kind of test: it guards a line that exists only because a general rule was wrong in one specific case, and it is the sort of rule a refactor is otherwise very happy to tidy away. You can check the whole thing from the outside, which is the nice part about prices being in the HTML: the figures are on the pricing page and repeated on the download page , with the currency note under each. What you are buying is on the per-site alert pages , such as Kamernet or Idealista , and the comparisons against the subscription services are at notifio.app/compare .

title: Seventeen words for eight database values, and a dot that only pulses when work is actually running
author: Daniel Pertu
summary: Nakodo does its work while nobody is watching: it reads a brand's website, finds creators and businesses who fit, writes the first email and handles the replies. The how it works page is the public version of that. The private version is a screen that has to answer, in about four words per row, what is happening right now. That answer lives in three small files totalling 106 lines. None of them touches the database, and none of the words in them is stored anywhere. Eight values, seventeen words The conversation table has a status column and a closed_reason column. Both are plain text with a TypeScript enum over them, because this app has no pgEnum anywhere. The words a human reads are a pair of records: export const STATUS_LABELS : Record < OutreachStatus , string > = { drafting : " Writing " , review : " To approve " , queued : " Scheduled " , contacted : " Contacted " , talking : " Talking " , needs_you : " Needs you " , handed_off : " Introduced " , closed : " Closed " , }; export const CLOSED_LABELS : Record < OutreachClosedReason , string > = { no_reply : " No reply " , declined : " Declined " , opted_out : " Opted out " , bounced : " Address bounced " , complained : " Marked as spam " , cancelled : " Stopped " , suppressed : " Can't be contacted " , no_email : " No email " , failed : " Failed " , }; export function threadLabel ( t : { status : OutreachStatus ; closedReason : OutreachClosedReason | null }): string { return t . status === " closed " && t . closedReason ? CLOSED_LABELS [ t . closedReason ] : STATUS_LABELS [ t . status ]; } Seventeen words for what the machine thinks of as eight states, and the reason is the three-line function at the bottom. A closed conversation that knows why it closed never shows the word "Closed", because "Closed" is a true statement that answers nothing. "No reply" and "Marked as spam" and "Opted out" are the same state to a scheduler and three completely different things to the person whose brand sent the email: one is normal, one is a deliverability problem, and one is a person telling you to stop. Typing both as Record<Union, string> rather than Record<string, string> is the whole safety net. Add a ninth closed reason to the schema and the build fails in this file until it has a word. That is the cheapest possible test for "no state reaches the UI without a human writing a sentence for it". Five views over eight statuses The same file groups them, in display order, with satisfies doing the checking: export const THREAD_VIEWS = [ { key : " attention " , label : " Needs you " , statuses : [ " needs_you " , " review " ] }, { key : " active " , label : " In progress " , statuses : [ " drafting " , " queued " , " contacted " , " talking " ] }, { key : " introduced " , label : " Introduced " , statuses : [ " handed_off " ] }, { key : " closed " , label : " Closed " , statuses : [ " closed " ] }, { key : " all " , label : " All " , statuses : null }, ] as const satisfies readonly { key : string ; label : string ; statuses : readonly OutreachStatus [] | null }[]; export type ThreadView = ( typeof THREAD_VIEWS )[ number ][ " key " ]; as const satisfies is the pairing I reach for most often in this codebase: as const keeps the literal types, so ThreadView is "attention" | "active" | ... derived from the data, and satisfies checks every status string against the schema union without widening anything. A plain type annotation would have given me string for the keys and no union to derive. Two things in that array are decisions rather than data. "Needs you" collapses two statuses, because a first email waiting for approval and a reply the model would not answer are both "a human has to look", and a product that makes you learn the difference before you can act has failed at the one job. And statuses: null for "All" means absent rather than a list of everything, so adding a status never silently drops it out of the one view that promises completeness. The badge is not a traffic light // A conversation's state. Introduced is the one stamp; anything waiting on // the brand is ochre-outlined; work in flight is plain ink; closed stays // quiet. No traffic-light colours. const TONE : Record < OutreachStatus , string > = { drafting : " border-dashed border-ink-400 text-muted-foreground " , review : " border-mark-outline text-foreground " , queued : " border-dashed border-foreground/50 text-foreground " , contacted : " border-foreground/60 text-foreground " , talking : " border-cyano-700 text-cyano-800 dark:border-cyano-300 dark:text-cyano-200 " , needs_you : " border-mark-outline bg-mark/30 text-foreground " , handed_off : " border-cyano-700 bg-cyano-50 text-cyano-800 dark:border-cyano-300 dark:bg-cyano-950 dark:text-cyano-200 " , closed : " border-ink-400/60 text-muted-foreground " , }; Eight tones, two hues, and no red or green anywhere. The brand document is blunt about why: ochre is "used only for attention marks", so the moment a colour means "danger" or "success" it stops meaning "look here". A closed conversation is not a failure, a reply is not an alarm, and three quarters of the states are neither good nor bad, so the axis the colours actually encode is "does this need you", not "is this going well". The signals are also doubled on purpose. Only two states get a fill, filled is "waiting on you" and "introduced", and the attention dot used elsewhere carries its own text: export function AttentionMark ({ label , className }: { label : string ; className ?: string }) { return ( < span className = { cn ( " inline-flex " , className ) } > < span className = "inline-block size-[7px] rounded-full border border-mark-outline bg-mark" aria-hidden = "true" /> < span className = "sr-only" > { label } </ span > </ span > ); } Seven pixels of ochre and a screen-reader sentence. The dot is decoration, the sr-only text is the information, which is the only arrangement that survives WCAG 1.4.1 and a colourblind reader. The dot that tells you whether anything is happening A campaign gets a different treatment: one word and a dot, where the dot answers a question the word cannot. export function LiveDot ({ live , label , className }: { live : boolean ; label : string ; className ?: string }) { return ( < span className = { cn ( " inline-flex items-center gap-1.5 text-[13px] text-muted-foreground " , className )} > < span className = " relative inline-flex size-1.5 " > { live && ( < span className = " absolute inset-0 rounded-full bg-cyano-600 motion-safe:animate-[live-pulse_2.4s_ease-out_infinite] " /> )} < span className = { cn ( " relative inline-flex size-1.5 rounded-full " , live ? " bg-cyano-600 " : " bg-ink-400 " )} / > < /span > < span className = { cn ( live && " text-foreground " )} > { label } < /span > < /span > ); } A solid dot with a pulsing copy behind it, motion-safe so it is a static dot for anybody who has asked for less motion, and the label's own colour as the second channel so the state is legible without the animation. And then the function that decides live , which is 32 lines and the densest product thinking in the app: // Campaign status as a live dot and a word. Only running work pulses: a // campaign with only its emails paused is still searching, and one with // enough good leads waiting may still be checking what it found. export function campaignStatus ( status : string , working : boolean , pauseMode : PauseMode | null = null , enoughLeads = false , ): { live : boolean ; label : string } { switch ( status ) { case " researching " : return { live : true , label : " Reading website " }; case " draft " : return { live : false , label : " Brief to review " }; case " active " : if ( enoughLeads ) return { live : working , label : " Enough leads " }; return working ? { live : true , label : " Surveying " } : { live : false , label : " Up to date " }; case " paused " : return pauseMode === " emails " ? { live : working , label : " Emails paused " } : pauseMode === " finding " ? { live : false , label : " Finding paused " } : { live : false , label : " Paused " }; case " failed " : return { live : false , label : " Research failed " }; default : return { live : false , label : status }; } } Four inputs, nine possible labels, six database statuses. The two branches worth staring at are the ones that return live: working rather than true or false . "Emails paused" with a pulsing dot looks wrong until you remember that pause here has a reason column and three answers: a campaign can be paused for sending while it carries on searching. The word tells you what is stopped, the dot tells you that something is still moving. If live were hardcoded false for every paused campaign, the screen would claim nothing is happening while jobs run, and the next thing that appears would be unexplained. "Up to date" versus "Surveying" is the same trick with the opposite emphasis: same status, same plan, and the only difference is whether any job is open right now. "Idle" would have been a worse word, because nothing is wrong, and "Active" would have been a worse word, because nothing is happening. The branch that should not exist default : return { live : false , label : status }; That line prints a raw database value into the interface. active instead of "Surveying", in lower case, in a dot label. It exists because the first parameter is typed status: string and not the schema's union, so TypeScript cannot see that the switch is exhaustive and insists on a return. Printing the raw value is the right behaviour for a branch that should be unreachable: it does not crash, it does not say "Unknown", and anybody who sees active on a card knows immediately that a status was added and this file was not told. But the honest fix is one word in the signature. Narrow status to the union, the switch becomes exhaustive, the default goes away, and the next person to add a status gets a compile error in the same place the conversation labels already give them one. Three files, 106 lines, 26 words, and not one of them in the database. The nearest public equivalent is the glossary , where the same discipline is applied to the words customers meet before they sign up: one definition each, written once, and never two names for one thing.

title: SEO Basics in 5 Minutes: What It Is and How Google Decides What to Show
author: Rachit Sharma
summary: If you build websites or run a business, someone has probably told you to "do your SEO". Here's the plain version. What is SEO? SEO means making your website easy for Google to find, understand and trust, so it shows up when people search. How Google works Crawl: Google visits your pages by following links. Index: Google saves what it found in its library. Rank: when someone searches, Google shows the pages it thinks answer best. If a page isn't crawled and indexed, it can't rank. Check that first. The 3 parts of SEO On-page is what's on your site: keywords, page content, titles and headings. Write for the question the person actually typed. Off-page is what others say about you: backlinks, reviews and mentions. Technical is whether Google can read your site: page speed, mobile friendliness, a sitemap and HTTPS. Work on all three. A great page on a broken site won't get far, and a fast site with thin content won't either. What's next This is Day 1 of a short SEO basics series. Day 2 is how to audit a business website. I'm a digital marketer from Kaithal, Haryana. What would you like me to cover?

title: I grepped for @ts-ignore and found zero. Then I grepped for the cast nobody bans
author: chet100
summary: Every TypeScript team has a rule about @ts-ignore . Ours does too, and it works: zero occurrences across 610 source files . Then I grepped for something nobody puts in a style guide: grep -rn --include = '*.ts' --include = '*.tsx' \ --exclude-dir = node_modules --exclude-dir = .next \ 'as unknown as' apps packages | wc -l 117. Zero explicit suppressions, a hundred and seventeen implicit ones. That ratio is not a coincidence — it is what a ban creates when the ban only covers the syntax people remember to grep for. The numbers, from a real repo Pattern Occurrences in source @ts-ignore 0 @ts-expect-error 0 as any 3 as unknown as 117 eslint-disable* 53 console.log 4 Two more facts worth having. The 53 eslint-disables are not 53 decisions: 42 of them are one rule ( @next/next/no-img-element ), which is a single architectural choice about tags, repeated. And the casts are not evenly spread — they cluster: File as unknown as api/src/routes/admin.ts 14 api/src/stories/worker.ts 11 api/src/app.ts 7 api/src/assistant/worker.ts 6 web/src/lib/messages/index.ts 5 api/src/stories/production.ts 5 That distribution tells you what the casts are for. Admin routes parse request payloads. Workers deserialise rows that came back from the database as unknown . The i18n map indexes strings by a computed key. These are all boundaries — the places where a runtime shape meets a compile-time type and nobody wrote the parser. Why this one survives code review as unknown as Foo is two casts. The first erases the type to unknown , which is honest; the second asserts it back to whatever you want, which is the lie. Together they are semantically identical to as any , with three advantages: It compiles under no-explicit-any . If your lint config bans any — most do — this is the way around it. It reads as deliberate. A reviewer skimming a diff sees a cast, not a suppression comment. There is no red flag to grep for in review. It is what an agent reaches for. When a model is asked to make a type error go away, as unknown as is the minimal edit that satisfies the compiler without adding a comment a human might question. That last one is why the count grows on AI-assisted branches. The tool is not malicious; it is doing exactly what it was asked. The ban list just does not cover the escape hatch it found. The gate I added A grep in CI, with an explicit allowlist file — because the goal is not zero this week, it is "never again 117". #!/usr/bin/env bash # fail when the double-cast count grows past the recorded budget budget = $( cat .cast-budget ) actual = $( grep -rn --include = '*.ts' --include = '*.tsx' \ --exclude-dir = node_modules --exclude-dir = .next \ 'as unknown as' apps packages | grep -v 'as-unknown-as-allow' | wc -l ) echo "as unknown as: ${ actual } (budget ${ budget } )" if [ " $actual " -gt " $budget " ] ; then echo "New double casts. Narrow the type, or add the line to the allowlist with a reason." exit 1 fi Three properties matter more than the rule itself: A budget, not a ban. A hard zero on day one means a 117-line allowlist nobody reads. A ratchet — budget goes down when you fix one, never up — keeps the number honest. The allowlist carries a reason. // as-unknown-as-allow: stripe webhook payload is validated upstream is a reviewable sentence. An empty allowlist entry is a comment that says nothing. It runs in the same job as typecheck , so the count is visible in the PR that changes it. If your setup has typescript-eslint installed, the equivalent rule is a restricted-syntax selector: ' no-restricted-syntax ' : [ ' error ' , { selector : ' TSAsExpression > TSUnknownKeyword ' , message : ' Double cast. Narrow with a parser or a guard instead. ' , }] I would still keep the grep: it works in repos with no ESLint, in CI scripts, and on the day the parser plugin upgrades and the selector stops matching. The three patterns behind 90% of them Reading the 117 by hand, they fall into three groups, each with a replacement that costs about ten minutes per file: 1. Parsing external data. JSON.parse(body) as unknown as JobRow becomes a schema parse at the boundary, and everything downstream is genuinely typed: const JobRow = z . object ({ id : z . string (), status : z . enum ([ ' queued ' , ' running ' , ' done ' ]) }); const row = JobRow . parse ( JSON . parse ( body )); // typed, and it fails loudly on drift 2. Reading database rows into a domain type. The cast moves the failure from "somewhere later, with a stack trace that does not mention the column" to "here, at the read". A small mapper function per table beats a cast per caller. 3. Indexing a translation map by a computed key. messages[key] as unknown as string usually wants satisfies Record on the definition and a typed accessor — the cast disappears because the shape was always there, just unproven. When the double cast is fine Test doubles. A partial implementation of a large interface is a cast-shaped problem; keep it in tests and let the budget ignore *.test.ts . Module augmentation for untyped third-party packages. You are asserting something the package should have declared. Put it in one types/ file with a comment, and it never needs to appear twice. Migration boundaries. When a column changes type, one cast with a // migration: remove after 2026-12 marker is cheaper than a parallel type tree. Everything else is a parser you did not write yet. FAQ Is as unknown as slower at runtime? No. TypeScript erases both casts; the cost is entirely in what the compiler stops checking. Does satisfies replace it? Sometimes. satisfies proves a value matches a type without widening it — which is exactly the i18n case — but it cannot rescue a value you did not construct. Why not ban it outright? Because a ban without a migration path produces an allowlist longer than the problem. The budget is the migration path. Would a stricter tsconfig catch these? noUncheckedIndexedAccess and exactOptionalPropertyTypes remove a chunk of the reasons people reach for a cast. They also produce a lot of red on day one. Ratchet the same way. The counts above came from one repository and one grep ; your ratio will differ, and the interesting number is the ratio, not the total. If you run the same audit and get zero double casts, I want to know what your boundaries look like, because that is a codebase with parsers everywhere.

title: Our homepage serves 24 logo elements for 12 logo files, and four more files nobody has ever requested
author: Daniel Pertu
summary: The CogniPrep landing page has a wall of company logos under the hero with the caption "Some companies that our clients have applied to". Twelve logos, three rows of four, about as simple as a component gets. Here is what the deployed HTML actually contains: curl -s https://cogniprep.app/ | grep -o ']*logos/[a-z-]*\.svg[^>]*>' | wc -l Every logo twice. Why there are two of each The hero is a two-column layout on desktop with the grid in the right column, and a single column on mobile with the grid underneath the buttons. One element cannot be in two places in the DOM, so the page does this: { /* Right Column - Company Grid */ } < div className = "animate-fade-in mt-8 hidden md:block" > < CompanyGrid /> { /* Mobile company grid */ } < div className = "animate-fade-in md:hidden" > < CompanyGrid /> hidden md:block and md:hidden , so exactly one is ever visible. This is a completely ordinary thing to write, and the cost is invisible until you count: 24 elements, 24 copies of the props in the streamed RSC payload, and the caption string appearing four times in one response (twice in the HTML, twice in the payload). The browser is fine about the bytes, because both copies point at the same 12 URLs and the second set is a cache hit.
